extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning how to write mathematical proofs (transition-to-proof courses)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for constructing clear, logically-structured proofs for typical undergraduate mathematics statements using templates keyed to logical form (universals, existentials, implications, conjunctions, disjunctions, negation, etc.). Emphasizes scope, indentation, and explicit handling of quantifiers and witnesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: To prove ∀x. P(x) (universal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Template: 'Let x be arbitrary. [Argue P(x).] Since x was arbitrary, ∀x. P(x).' Choose the variable name to avoid clash. Don't make any assumption about x beyond its type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start by introducing an arbitrary element of the domain; avoid naming clashes with existing variables; do not assume any special property of x except its declared type. Make the quantifier scope explicit by stating 'let x be arbitrary' and conclude by invoking the arbitrariness to generalize.

rubrics_metrics.name: To prove ∃x. P(x) (existential)
rubrics_metrics.description: Template: 'Let x = [the witness you have in mind]. We show P(x). [Verify.]' Often you find the witness by working backward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide an explicit witness before using it in arguments. If the witness is not obvious, work backward from the goal to construct it. Verify the property P(x) for that witness; do not assume existence without presenting a witness.

rubrics_metrics.name: To prove P ⇒ Q (implication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Template: 'Suppose P. [Argue Q.] Since Q followed from P, the implication holds.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin a new scope by assuming the antecedent. All reasoning that depends on this assumption should be clearly indented or marked. At the end, explicitly state that Q follows from the assumption, discharging the assumption to conclude the implication.

rubrics_metrics.name: To prove P ⇔ Q (biconditional)
rubrics_metrics.description: Template: Two separate proofs. 'First, suppose P … so Q. Conversely, suppose Q … so P.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Split the biconditional into two independent directions and prove each with the appropriate template (typically implication proofs). Make clear which direction is being proved and keep scopes for each direction separate.

rubrics_metrics.name: To prove P ∧ Q (conjunction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Template: 'We prove P and Q separately. (a) [Prove P.] (b) [Prove Q.]'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate each conjunct in its own subproof or paragraph. Label or separate the subproofs so the reader can see both components have been established.

rubrics_metrics.name: To prove P ∨ Q (disjunction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Template (case split): 'Either R or not-R. Case 1: R … so P. Case 2: not-R … so Q. In either case, P ∨ Q.' Or: assume not-P, derive Q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an exhaustive case analysis or a direct derivation (e.g., prove ¬P ⇒ Q). When using case splits, ensure cases are exhaustive and preferably disjoint; make the reasoning in each case explicit and conclude the disjunction after treating all cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: To prove ¬P (negation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Template: 'Suppose, for contradiction, P. [Derive an absurdity.] Therefore ¬P.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce a temporary assumption P and derive a contradiction (an absurdity or an outright false statement). Then discharge the assumption to conclude the negation. Make the contradiction clear and explain why it cannot hold.

rubrics_metrics.name: To use ∀x. P(x) (universal as hypothesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the hypothesis by applying it to a specific x = c. Then P(c) holds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When you have a universal hypothesis, instantiate it on a particular element of the domain to obtain the corresponding instance. State the instantiation explicitly (e.g., 'by ∀x P(x) with x = c, we get P(c)').

rubrics_metrics.name: To use ∃x. P(x) (existential as hypothesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose x0 such that P(x0). [Treat x0 as a known new constant.]
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an existential is given, introduce a fresh name for a witness and proceed under the assumption that the witness satisfies the property. Be careful not to conflate this fresh constant with arbitrary elements; its scope is limited to the subproof where the witness is used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indentation and scope must mirror logical structure
rubrics_metrics.description: The proof should visibly mirror its logical form: indentation tracks logical depth. Each 'Suppose' / 'Let arbitrary' opens a scope. Every scope must close with the conclusion that depends on it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visually structure proofs so nested assumptions and conclusions are clear (indentation, boxed scopes, or explicit markers). Always close scopes by discharging assumptions and explicitly stating what was concluded from that scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start with the right setup for the statement's logical form
rubrics_metrics.description: Checklist item: Does the proof start with the right setup for the statement's logical form?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the outermost logical operators (quantifiers, implications, conjunctions, etc.) in the theorem statement and begin the proof with the template that matches that logical form (e.g., introduce an arbitrary element for a universal, assume antecedent for implication).

rubrics_metrics.name: Make quantifier scopes explicit
rubrics_metrics.description: Checklist item: Are quantifier scopes explicit?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly indicate where quantifiers are instantiated or introduced; avoid implicit scope shifts. Use phrases like 'let x be arbitrary', 'for this fixed x', or explicit instantiations 'apply ∀x to x = a' to show scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discharge assumptions at end of their scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Checklist item: Are assumptions discharged at the end of their scope?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure every temporary assumption (from 'suppose', 'assume', 'let') is explicitly discharged when concluding the subproof, and state the resulting implication or quantified conclusion that follows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case splits must be exhaustive and disjoint
rubrics_metrics.description: Checklist item: Are case splits exhaustive and disjoint?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When splitting into cases, verify that the cases cover all possibilities (exhaustive) and, when relevant, that they do not overlap (disjoint). State the cases and why they are exhaustive; handle each case separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existential witnesses must be produced before use
rubrics_metrics.description: Checklist item: Are existential witnesses produced before being used?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Never use an existentially-claimed object without first presenting or fixing a witness. Introduce a witness with a fresh name and verify it satisfies the required property before employing it in further reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure of the proof should match structure of the statement
rubrics_metrics.description: Checklist item: Does the structure of the proof match the structure of the statement?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize the order and nesting of subproofs to reflect the logical composition of the theorem (e.g., show two directions for a biconditional, separate proofs for conjuncts, nested scopes for combined quantifiers and implications). This aids clarity and correctness.
